sections.html:
Previously on…

Ask a player to recap S51, then fill gaps with:

  • Darius named the symbol: the Umbral Order. Gideon said the names in the old ballad, Zara, Rilien, Galtor and the rest, are titles of something divine. Nobody knows what that means yet.
  • Lira traced the Order to the Whisperwind Halls at the Econa's headwaters. Inkwich is the nearest teleport.
  • Korin, Lira and 14 soldiers came with you. You still have the house on Sable Lane. And somewhere in Inkwich, Sfillian's brother Leath is a captive.

Decide before you run

  • Lirien is the crow new: the crow that watches the party all day is Lirien's herald-shape, and its speaking pays off the jacket's first whisper. Keep or drop.
  • Why Lirien sought the party [OPEN]. Proposal: Iaru whispered "find the sword that dreams," which is Daehir. Lirien and Daehir met at Bantambar new.
  • Names: this page treats Rilien as Kassis's emissary (evil) and Eone's as Raffa. The codex lists Rilien under both [CONFLICT].
  • Do the Caldwells already know Lewis is dead? (Scene 4 assumes not.)
  • Lewis's unfinished contract: the target. And party level, if the DCs need tuning.

The day at a glance

Scene 1 sets up the day. Scenes 2 to 4 happen in daylight, in any order, though the tower must be found before Lirien's half of Scene 4. Scene 5 happens at dusk and ends the session on Leath.

sections.title: Homecoming
sections.html:
1

Homecoming

MorningAugury safehouse → Sable Lane
Who: Korin, Lira, Sgt. Hal Brisk, 14 soldiers, Pip Tallow, Marta Fenn, a crowLeans on: Sfillian Richter Ash
Why they're here

The S51 cliffhanger: Lira teleports everyone to the Augury's Inkwich circle. The party offered their house as the staging area, so the walk home to Sable Lane is the natural first move, and the missing tower stops them on the way.

Art prompt · The Augury safehouse

Painterly fantasy concept art, warm late-summer light over a river-trade city, muted earth tones with bright silk accents and an uncanny emerald-green undertone, soft atmospheric haze, cinematic composition, highly detailed environment, 16:9 aspect ratio. A large, dim stone chamber in an old river-trade city, used in secret as a teleportation waypoint. A well-worn teleportation circle is inlaid in the flagstone floor, its carved runes fading from soft white-gold to a dying ember glow, the grooves polished smooth by decades of arrivals. Heavy stone walls hung with faded tapestries of interlocking triangles and hexagons in dusty blues and ochres. Thin ribbons of incense smoke curl through a single shaft of pale morning light falling from a high slit window, dust motes hanging in it. A worn wooden lectern by the door holds an open logbook and a crusted inkpot. At the far end, a heavy iron-banded oak door stands slightly ajar, a bright sliver of sunlit street beyond it, and on the carved lintel above it a single black crow sits watching. Quiet, watchful, secretive mood; cool stone grays warmed by gold light, a faint electric shimmer in the air above the circle. No people, no text, no watermark.

Art prompt · Sable Lane

Painterly fantasy concept art, warm late-summer light over a river-trade city, muted earth tones with bright silk accents and an uncanny emerald-green undertone, soft atmospheric haze, cinematic composition, highly detailed environment, 16:9 aspect ratio. A narrow cobblestone residential lane climbing one of a river city's seven hills, lined with timber-and-plaster townhouses that lean toward each other over the street like old friends sharing a secret, their upper stories so close that lines of white laundry are strung between the windows and snapping in the breeze. Window boxes overflow with marigolds gone to dry seed. In the center, one modest, too-narrow, too-tall two-story house with peeling green paint and heavy new iron locks on its door; a single black crow perches on its brass knocker. A broom leans against a neighbor's freshly swept step. Above the rooftops in the distance, on the tallest hill, a grand honey-colored temple with a ribbed dome and one soaring bell tower; beside it, a stump sliced perfectly flat where a second tower should be, its cut face glinting faintly copper-green in the sun. Early morning light, long soft shadows, gentle haze over the hills. No people, no text, no watermark.

Soundtrack prompt · Homecoming

An orchestral ambient soundtrack of a homecoming to a river-trade city on a late-summer morning, performed by a live chamber orchestra: warm violins and violas, a gentle solo oboe over rippling concert harp, soft tubular bells in the distance, then a slow turn toward unease as low cellos and double basses sustain one dark, held note beneath. Wistful, nostalgic, a little haunted. 70 BPM, D major drifting toward D minor. Real acoustic instruments, concert-hall reverb, no synthesizers, no pads, no electronic sounds. Loopable, instrumental, no vocals.

Cold open

Lira's voice is the last thing you hear in Harmonia: a soft, rising chant, the syllables stacking one on another like stones in an arch. The runes under your feet kindle, white-gold and humming, and then the world folds. There's a feeling like missing a step in the dark, a roar like the sea in a shell, a taste of copper on your tongue. Then stone under your boots again, and silence.

You're standing in a large, dim room hung with tapestries of interlocking triangles and hexagons in faded blues and ochres. The air is thick with incense and old parchment, and threaded through both is the faint electric fizz of spent magic, raising the hair on your arms. The circle beneath you fades from gold to ember to nothing; its grooves are worn smooth by decades of arrivals. With a sound like a held breath let go, Korin and fourteen soldiers blink into being around you, armor clanking, someone swearing quietly.

Beyond the heavy door, a city is waking. You step out, and Inkwich washes over you like warm water: fresh bread from a bakery on the corner, where a flour-dusted woman is stacking loaves in the window; hooves on cobblestone; shutters banging open up and down the street; a man with a spectacular hangover being cheerfully mocked by his friend. "Morning, Deitrich! Didn't think we'd see you upright!" Fourteen soldiers fall into step behind you, and the street turns to stare. On the carved lintel above the door you've just come out of, a crow is sitting very still, its head cocked, watching you. When you glance back a moment later, it hasn't moved. When you glance back again, it's gone.

Underneath the ordinary noise, something is wrong. People stand in twos and threes, voices low, and they keep glancing up toward the hill. "…did you hear…?" "…gone, I'm telling you, just gone…" "…woke up and the whole sky was green…" The closer you get to Sable Lane, the more every conversation in the city sounds like the same conversation.

You turn onto the broad street that climbs toward the old quarter, the view opens, and you see it. The Temple of Ouna has stood on its hilltop longer than anyone can remember, two great bell towers raised either side of its dome like hands lifted in blessing. You've used it to find your way home a hundred times. One of the hands is gone. Where the eastern tower soared there is a stump, and the morning sun strikes its top and flashes back at you like a mirror. The light it throws is green.

Korin stops beside you. "That," he says quietly, "is no coincidence."

Sable Lane

Sable Lane looks like it was built by people who liked each other. The townhouses lean in over the cobbles like old friends sharing a secret, close enough that neighbors string laundry between the windows, and this morning a row of white sheets is snapping in the river breeze like the sails of a ship that never leaves port. A woman in a blue headscarf is sweeping her front step with the slow rhythm of someone who has swept it every morning for forty years. She stops, broom in hand, to stare at fourteen soldiers marching down her lane.

Your house looks exactly as you left it: a little too narrow, a little too tall, the heavy iron locks Lewis insisted on still gleaming against the peeling green paint. The marigolds Nancy Caldwell planted in the window boxes have bloomed and died and gone to seed, and the dry stalks rattle faintly against the glass. A crow is perched on the brass knocker. It looks at you as if it has been waiting for someone to come home, and when you climb the step it hops politely aside to let you reach the lock.

Inside, the air is cool and still and smells of cedar and dust and, faintly, of all of you: old pipe smoke, oiled leather, the ghost of a stew someone burned months ago. Light comes sideways through the shutters and lays golden bars across the floor. Upstairs, four doors line the hall. Three of them are just doors. The fourth, front right, is Lewis's, and it is closed.

The task list

Within ten minutes, Sergeant Hal Brisk has assigned bunks by rank, someone has found the kettle, and someone else has found the mouse and is chasing it around the kitchen with a helmet. The house that has been silent for months is suddenly full of life, and it isn't your life, and it's strange how much that stings.

Korin has claimed the kitchen. He's unrolled a long map of the Econa across your table, weighting its corners with a teapot, a dagger, a boot and a heel of bread, and folded himself into a chair that was never built for a Leonin. He runs one broad finger up the blue line of the river, past the names of towns you've never heard of, all the way into the mountains where the line frays and stops. Then he looks up, gold eyes bright.

"I'll see to the boat and the docks. I'd rather row in shifts and never make camp. Lira has the safehouse to settle." He spreads his hands. "This is your city, not mine. What is on everyone's task list?"

Hand out the day's leads here. Let the players build the list; make sure these surface:

  • Lira, quietly, to Dr. Sharpfoot: "I want your eyes on that tower before anyone else touches it. You see what the rest of us decide not to." → Scene 2.
  • Korin's supply list: rope, oars, rations for twenty, healing draughts. The Caldwells have supplied the party since S4. → Scene 4.
  • Korin, to Richter: "Your father was a smith, Lira tells me. Did he ever speak of the Stonesunder?" (Wait for the answer. It seeds Richter's thread.)
  • The crow moves from the knocker to the chimney to the lamppost across the lane, always watching. Marta Fenn: "That bird's been on your knocker since dawn, dear." → Scene 3, if they follow it.
  • Then the knock at the door (below) → Scene 5, at dusk.

The note arrives

Someone knocks at the front door: three quick raps, a pause, then two more, like the opening of a song. Sergeant Brisk opens it with one hand on his sword. On the step is a boy of about ten, with a gap where his front teeth should be, bare feet black with street dirt and a cap three sizes too big. He takes one look at the sergeant's armor and decides to talk to someone else.

"Delivery for the bard." His eyes land on Sfillian. "That's you, innit? Jacket like that, has to be." He holds out a folded square of heavy cream paper sealed with plain red wax, then snatches it back an inch. "Gent said it was paid. But I reckon it's worth another copper to deliver it."

Handout · the note
Your brother sends his regards.
Silkcliff, at dusk.
Come and hear the last verse.

Unsigned, in an elegant old-fashioned hand. A single lute string is coiled inside.

Druder's Note
Loot · gear

The note and its silver-wound lute string, for Sfillian's inventory.

The paper · DC 12 Investigation

Held to the light: a watermark of a silk moth, wings spread. Expensive paper, the kind rich houses use. (Foreshadows how Druder leaves in Scene 5.)

The string · DC 15 History or Performance

Gut wound with silver wire: a stringing only old troubadours from the Scarsend valley still use. Shortcliff troubadours. A hint, not a reveal. (Sfillian has advantage.)

Who sent you?RoleplayDC 12 Persuasion · Intimidation · or a copper

Pip Tallow shifts from foot to foot, eyeing the soldiers and the copper. What do you ask him, and how?

Success

Pip pockets it and leans in, delighted to be important. "Gent in a long coat, purple-ish, like a plum gone off. Fancy, but worn at the cuffs. Smelled of wine and lamp oil. Kept one arm tucked in his cloak the whole time, like he was cold, but it ain't cold." He grins his gap-toothed grin. "Paid me a whole silver. Said the show starts at dusk."

Failure

Pip's eyes go wide at something over your shoulder. When you turn back, he's halfway down Sable Lane, your copper in his fist, shouting without slowing: "Your brother says hello! Show's at dusk!"

Cost: no description of the sender. They still have the note.

Lewis's room optional

The room is exactly as he left it. The bed is made with the tight corners of someone taught by a mother who checked. His spare boots stand side by side under the window. On the desk: a dried-up quill, an inkpot gone to crust, and a half-eaten apple shrunk to a brown wrinkled fist. Light falls through the shutters in thin gold lines, and the dust turns slowly in it, and nothing else moves at all.

Quick reference · Sable Lane house
Look closerA Minstrel's Refrain letter for Sfillian, asking for news of the "green star." Mouse droppings; a chewed map corner. Rooms as in S15: Lewis front right, Sfillian rear right, Richter front left, Ash rear left.
HiddenDC 14 Investigation or anyone who remembers: Lewis's false-bottom drawer holds an unfinished Hidden Hand Grip contract [OPEN] target? and a small portrait of his sister Violet.
SensesDust in gold light · dry seed stalks rattling on glass · cedar and old pipe smoke · the cold brass of Ash's fifth key
Who's hereSgt. Hal Brisk: dry humor, sleeps sitting up against doors.Pip Tallow: ten, gap-toothed, sells everything twice.Marta Fenn: neighbor in the blue headscarf; saw "a gentleman in a plum coat" watching the house two evenings ago.The crow: knocker, chimney, lamppost; it's Lirien (Scene 3).
On returnAfter the party leaves upriver: Thomas Caldwell checks the house weekly and leaves potions with notes about their side effects.

Ask the table

  • Sfillian, when did you last see Leath, and what was he doing?
  • Whoever opens Lewis's door: what's the first thing you touch?
  • What has each of you missed about Inkwich?

If the party…

Shows Korin the noteHe offers soldiers. If they bring them, Druder sees them coming and skips straight to the reveal (Scene 5).
Heads to Silkcliff nowThe top hut is locked, the cage on its crane wrapped in silk. Old Bett Loom says the "silk buyer" only comes at dusk.
Tries to catch the crowIt's never quite where they grab. It lands just out of reach, looks east, and waits.
Leads to · Scene 2 · 3 · 43 paths
To the temple hillGo to Scene 2 →

NudgeLira, to Dr. Sharpfoot: "Before the Faffors trample it." Korin sends two soldiers as an escort through the crowds.

You leave Sable Lane and start to climb. Inkwich is built on seven hills, and each one wears a different century: timber gables on this one, red-tiled villas on the next, crumbling merchant walls on the third, where rich families once fortified their own small kingdoms. Korin's soldiers clatter along behind you, drawing stares from shopkeepers rolling up their shutters. Twice the temple hill vanishes behind the rooftops; twice it swings back into view as the street turns, closer each time. Then the houses fall away, and you're standing at the foot of the tallest hill, where the streets give up and the stairs begin.

Then read the Scene 2 arrival.

Following the crowGo to Scene 3 →

NudgeWhen the party steps outside, the crow flies a little way east, lands, and looks back. Marta Fenn: "It's waiting for you, dear. Crows know who owes them." Following it skips the temple's clues and leads straight to the tower.

The crow leads you east, one rooftop at a time. It never flies far: a chimney, a gutter, a cart's tailboard, a washing line that sags under it and swings. Each time you catch up, it waits, cocks its head, and goes on. Downhill, the houses shrink and the warehouses grow; iron grates in the street breathe cold air up from the river buried beneath you. Past the last warehouse, the cobbles give out into a dirt track and the city's noise drops behind you like a coat you've taken off. The crow settles on a fence post, looks at you one last time, and is gone. Ahead, the path drops through a stand of willows toward the water.

Then read the Scene 3 arrival.

To the Caldwell storeGo to Scene 4 →

NudgeKorin reads his list aloud: "Rope. Oars. Rations for twenty, two weeks. Healing draughts." Whoever has lived here says it before they think: the Caldwells.

You cut across the hillside toward the edge of the trade ward, through streets you could walk with your eyes closed. You know which cobble wobbles. You know the baker on the corner burns his rye on Tuesdays, and from the smell of it, he's done it again. A knife-grinder you remember is still working the same corner, sparks spinning off his wheel, and he lifts his chin to you as if you'd only been gone a day. Then you turn the last corner.

Then read the Scene 4 arrival.

sections.title: Where the Tower Stood
sections.html:
2

Where the Tower Stood

Late morningTemple of Ouna, the hilltop
Who: High Priestess Maren Oakhallow, Brother Calloway, Wren Ashby, Sgt. Odda KellLeans on: Sharpfoot Ash Richter
Why they're here
  • Lira asked Dr. Sharpfoot to look before anyone else touches it.
  • The party has carried a prayer book to Ouna since the Brass Knives ambush (S3). This is its home.
  • The whole city is climbing the hill. It's the only thing anyone is talking about.

The scene's job: point the party east, toward the river. Three witnesses each give one piece; any one of them is enough.

Art prompt · Temple of Ouna

Painterly fantasy concept art, warm late-summer light over a river-trade city, muted earth tones with bright silk accents and an uncanny emerald-green undertone, soft atmospheric haze, cinematic composition, highly detailed environment, 16:9 aspect ratio. A grand temple of pale honey-colored stone crowning the tallest of a city's seven hills, with a great ribbed dome and two bell towers flanking its doors like hands raised in blessing. The western tower soars intact, its bell visible in the open belfry. The eastern tower is gone: in its place stands a stump about forty feet high, sliced perfectly level as if by a single impossible stroke, its cut face melted into a skin of glass veined with the pale copper-green of verdigris, catching the sun like a mirror and throwing a faint green light across the square. No rubble anywhere; the flagstones are clean and whole. Wide temple steps strewn with offerings: candle stubs, wilting bundles of lilac, colored ribbons knotted to the iron railings and fluttering in the breeze. A simple rope cordon around the base of the stump. Pigeons wheeling over the empty square; the red rooftops of the city falling away below toward a river glinting in the east. Hazy morning sun, an uneasy, holy stillness. No people, no text, no watermark.

Soundtrack prompt · Where the Tower Stood

An orchestral ambient soundtrack of a wounded hilltop temple at midday, performed by a live string orchestra: slow, hushed divisi violins and violas, a solo cello line like a whispered prayer, distant sustained French horns, a single tubular bell struck now and then, and a quiet, unresolved celesta figure that sounds holy and incomplete. Reverent, uneasy, sacred stillness. 60 BPM, Dorian mode. Real acoustic instruments, concert-hall reverb, no synthesizers, no pads, no electronic sounds. Loopable, instrumental, no vocals.

The climb to the temple is the oldest road in Inkwich, worn into a gentle groove by a thousand years of feet, and this morning it's crowded the way it only is on high holy days. But nobody is singing. People climb in a hush, clutching candles and bundles of lilac and little knots of colored ribbon, and when they reach the top they stop, and look up, and stay there.

Where the eastern tower stood there is a stump perhaps forty feet high, and it ends in a cut so perfectly flat it looks less like damage than like a decision. The stone along the cut has melted and cooled into a skin of glass, veined through with a pale, chalky green, the color of an old copper roof. The sun strikes it and throws a light across the square that isn't quite white.

That's the first thing that's wrong. The second takes longer to notice. There is no rubble. A tower that tall should have buried half the square when it fell. But the flagstones are swept and whole, and the pigeons are pecking at spilled grain where the stones should be. The tower didn't fall. It simply isn't here anymore.

Faffor guards have roped off the base, looking like men who'd rather be guarding something they understood. The faithful have built a little shoreline of offerings on the steps: candle stubs, wilting flowers, ribbons fluttering on the railings. And threading through the incense and the hot-stone smell are two things that don't belong. Lilac, sweet and out of season, as if someone had walked through here carrying an armful of it. And under it, sharp and metallic, the smell of a fistful of old copper pennies.

The High Priestess

From the shadow of the temple doors comes a woman in ash-gray vestments, walking slowly, as if she's been up all night, which she has. Silver hair pinned back severely; a calm that is a discipline rather than a nature; her left hand wrapped in a clean white bandage. Passing the stump, she lays her good hand against it without looking, the way you'd touch a friend's shoulder at a funeral.

Then she sees you, and her eyes go, of all places, to the satchel with the worn little prayer book in it. She goes very still. "You carry one of ours. I'd know that binding anywhere. Where did you get it?"

High Priestess Maren Oakhallow new
Head of the Temple of Ouna · Neutral → Friendly if they tell the prayer book's story
Voice
Calm; keeps touching the bell rope while she talks
Wants
To know whether her goddess is angry
Hiding
She saw it happen, and heard a name. To the Faffors she claims she was asleep (DC 14 Insight).

"Ouna does not take. She weaves. This was taken."

The witnessRoleplayAuto with the prayer book's story · else DC 14 Persuasion (DC 12 after an offering)

She leads you into the nave, cool and dim after the glare, and sits beneath a stained-glass window of a woman at a loom. She doesn't look at you while she speaks. She looks up the stairwell, where daylight pours down from a ceiling that isn't there.

Success

"A little after midnight. I couldn't sleep; I was walking the cloister. The light came first: green, so bright the shadows went the wrong way. Then it was in the tower. A shape in the belfry, like a person made of light, sitting cross-legged on the bell as if it were a cushion. It said one word. A name: Iaru. I have read every prayer in this temple, and that name is in none of them." She turns her bandaged palm over in her lap. "Then a sound like a harp string snapping, and the tower was gone. It didn't fall. It went east. I felt it go, the way you feel a door close in another room."

Failure

"I've told the Faffors. I'll tell you. I was asleep." Her face is a closed door. But as she rises, a girl of about thirteen in an acolyte's smock, who has been sweeping the same three flagstones near you for several minutes, catches your eye and jerks her head toward the cloister: follow me.

Cost: Oakhallow stays Neutral and the name stays secret for now. Wren Ashby tells what she saw from the dormitory window: "The green light went east, and low, like someone carrying a lantern across the river."

Anyone who asks about "Iaru": DC 20 Religion or History recalls a name struck through in the oldest temple rolls, one of the gods the old texts call "the quiet ones." Nobody alive prays to him.

The bell-ringer

An old man in a brown habit is sitting on the bottom step of the empty stairwell, staring at his hands. The palms are raw, striped with rope burn. Brother Calloway has rung the bells of Ouna for fifty years, and he's deaf in one ear for it. He turns his good ear toward you. "I had the rope in my hands. Midnight bell. And the rope went slack, and the bell rang anyway. Not up there." He points, unerringly, east. "Out there. Over water. Bells sound different over water, son. Rounder. I've rung bells fifty years. I know where a bell is."

The cutDC 15 Arcana or ReligionSharpfoot: advantage with his tools

Sergeant Odda Kell sighs at the Augury badges and lifts the rope. Up close, the cut is level the way water is level, the way nothing a mason makes ever is. How do you approach it?

Success

The glass is warm, blood-warm, and beneath the warmth is a faint, slow pulse, like a heartbeat heard through a wall. It's holy; it has the clean, humming stillness of a consecrated altar. But it isn't Ouna's. Her presence is all through this temple, patient as a hand at a loom. This is something older and quieter, that arrived from very far away. And the green in the glass isn't paint or flame. It's verdigris: the bloom that grows on copper when it has been left a very, very long time.

Failure

The glass is warm and smooth and tells you nothing you can name. But the lilac is so strong at the cut it's almost dizzying, and a memory stirs: a night in Ironharbor, a green streak across the stars, and a garden of lilac outside an apothecary shop.

Cost: no divine reading. They still get the Ironharbor connection.

The shard · DC 16 Perception, DC 13 Sleight of Hand

A finger-long sliver of green-veined glass worked loose from the cut, warm as a living thing. In Richter's hand, Richterstorm hums. Caught by Odda Kell: "Hand it over, or the Strings get to call the Augury temple-robbers." A 5 gp bribe ends it.

The stairwell · DC 12 Athletics

The spiral stair climbs into open sky. From the top, the third clue: the herons over the river (read-aloud below).

Daehir stirs Ashvoice changer on

Something stirs at the edge of your mind, Ash, slow and enormous, like a great beast turning over in its sleep: a cold weight behind your eyes, the hilt-memory of a thousand battles. When his voice comes, it's quieter than you've ever heard it. "I know this cut." A long silence; you feel him reaching for something and failing to grasp it. "Not a blade. A staff. I have seen it made before, in the last war. I cannot remember the hand that held it." Then, almost to himself: "But I remember that I was afraid of it."

From the top of the stairwell

The stair simply stops, and you're standing on the top step with the whole sky over your head. The city lies below you like a map: red rooftops, the seven hills, and to the east the river, running open and gold beyond the last warehouses before it dives beneath the streets. In the middle of that open stretch is a long, low island of pale sand and reeds. Above it, wheeling slowly in a wide gray ring, are herons: dozens of them, circling and circling, as though there were something on the island they won't land on. Beside you, the bell rope sways, tied to nothing. Its frayed end, as the wind pushes it, points east.

Quick reference · Temple of Ouna
Look closerThe glass is warm hours later. Inside, the stairwell spirals to open sky. The bell rope hangs from nothing, its end frayed as if pulled hard.
SensesGreen-tinted light · a hush; a rope creaking with no bell · hot stone, lilac, old copper · warm glass · a sweetness in the air, like honey
Who's hereBrother Calloway: elderly bell-ringer, deaf in one ear, rope-burned palms. Heard the bell ring east, over water.Wren Ashby: acolyte, thirteen; saw the light go east and low over the river.Sgt. Odda Kell: Faffor, bored, bribable, wants her shift over.
Rumors"Ouna took it back" (false) · "The Strings sold the stone" (false: there's no stone) · "A green star fell on it" (true) · "The bell rang at midnight after the tower was gone" (true: from the eyot)
On returnAfter Lirien returns the tower (Scene 3): the stump is whole again, the seam a hairline of green glass. Pilgrims come from the countryside to touch it.

Ask the table

  • Ash: does Daehir's fear frighten you, or make you curious?

You take the eastern stair down off the temple hill, a long switchback of worn steps where washerwomen have pegged sheets across the landings, and you duck between them, the linen cool and damp against your faces. Halfway down, the incense fades behind you. At the bottom the warehouses rise on either side, and the iron grates underfoot breathe cold air up from the buried river. You keep walking east until the cobbles give out into a dirt track and the city's noise falls away behind you. Ahead, the path drops through a stand of willows toward the water.

The road down from the temples spills you out at the edge of the trade ward, and your feet know the way before your head does. Past the cooper's, past the stall that sells hot chestnuts in winter and cold cider in summer, past the Faffor post where the same tired guard has leaned on the same post for a year. He squints at you, decides you're not his problem, and goes back to leaning. Then you turn the last corner.

sections.title: The Herald in the Bell
sections.html:
3

The Herald in the Bell

AfternoonStillwater Eyot, the open Econa
Who: Lirien, Herald of Iaru; Mags Pellow; the heronsLeans on: everyone, especially Ash and Sfillian
Why they're here
  • The temple's clues all point east, over the river (Scene 2), or Senro's sailor's eye does (Scene 4).
  • Or they simply followed the crow (Scene 1).

The scene's job: the heart of the session. The tower is here, but it can only be seen by people who stop and stand still. Iaru is the god of meditation. Then the crow speaks, Lirien arrives, and the party gets its first real lesson in what the gods are.

Art prompt · Stillwater Eyot & the tower

Painterly fantasy concept art, warm late-summer light over a river-trade city, muted earth tones with bright silk accents and an uncanny emerald-green undertone, soft atmospheric haze, cinematic composition, highly detailed environment, 16:9 aspect ratio. A long, low island of pale sand and tall reeds in the middle of a wide, slow river, the water around it unnaturally glassy and still while the current ripples beyond. In the center of the island, rising out of a perfect ring of flattened reeds as if it had grown there, stands a single complete temple bell tower of honey-colored stone, seventy feet tall, its base sunk into the sand, with no temple attached to it. At its top, an open belfry holds a great green-bronze bell, perfectly motionless. Grey herons stand on its window ledges and on one leg in the shallows, utterly still. A flat-bottomed punt is drawn up at the island's edge. Far behind, on the near bank, willows and the last warehouses of a city on seven hills; upstream, a pale cliff strung with silk threads. Late afternoon gold light, fine haze over the water, a few lilac petals floating motionless on the surface. Serene, uncanny and holy. No people, no text, no watermark.

Soundtrack prompt · Stillwater Eyot

An orchestral ambient soundtrack of a still, enchanted river island where time slows down, performed by a small live orchestra: very soft sustained low strings, high violin harmonics, a slow alto flute melody, bowed crotales and a deep tubular bell that rings and fades, almost no rhythm, long rests between phrases, swelling and receding like breathing. Meditative, sacred, uncanny calm. 50 BPM, Lydian mode. Real acoustic instruments, concert-hall reverb, no synthesizers, no pads, no electronic sounds. Loopable, instrumental, no vocals.

Beyond the willows, the Econa opens out, and the noise of Inkwich falls away behind you as if a door has closed. Here, east of the last warehouses, the river runs wide and slow under the open sky: brown in the middle, gold where the light lies on it, green at the edges where the reeds grow thick enough to hide a boat. Dragonflies stitch back and forth over the shallows. Somewhere a frog is complaining.

In the middle of the river, perhaps a hundred yards out, lies a long, low island of pale sand and reeds. Every child in Inkwich knows it: Stillwater Eyot, where the herons stand. On any other day there would be dozens of them on it, gray and patient, each balanced on one leg in the shallows like an old man waiting for a cart. Today there isn't a single heron on the island. They're above it, all of them, circling in a slow, wide wheel, around and around, refusing to land.

A flat-bottomed punt is pulled up on the mud below the willows, and a broad woman in a man's hat is sitting in it, eating an onion like an apple. She looks at you, at the island, back at you. "You want the eyot." It isn't a question. "Herons won't go near it since midnight. Neither will I." A crunch of onion. "Two coppers and I'll put you on the sand. I'm not getting out."

The crossing is wrong in a way that takes a while to name. Halfway over, the current simply stops. The river goes glassy around the punt; the pole slides in and out of the water without a sound; a single lilac petal turns slowly on the surface beside you and does not drift. Then the sand of the eyot is under your boots, and there is nothing here. Sand. Reeds. Driftwood bleached white. A thousand heron prints, all of them leading away. And in the center of the island, a perfect ring of flattened reeds some thirty feet across, as if something enormous and heavy had been set down very gently.

There's nothing here. And yet there's a sound, if sound is the word: a note too low to hear, pressing on your breastbone and humming in your back teeth, like a bell rung long ago that never quite stopped. Above you the herons wheel, and wheel, and wheel. There's nothing here, and everything in you is saying there is.

Be stillGroup DC 13 Wisdom (Insight, Perception or Religion)Auto-success: the whole table goes silent for a slow count of ten

The note hums in your chest. The herons wheel. Something here is waiting for you to do the one thing you haven't done all day. What do you do?

If nobody thinks of stopping, a heron drops out of the wheel, lands at the water's edge, and stands on one leg, perfectly motionless, looking at them (DC 10 Insight: it's waiting). If the players get it, ask everyone at the table to stay silent while you count to ten, for real.

Success

One by one, you stop. Not just your feet: your hands, your voices, the small restless habits you didn't know you had. In the silence the low note becomes the only thing in the world, and you realize it was never one note. It's a breath. In, and out. In, and out. Somewhere in the middle of the third breath you understand that you've been looking at the tower the whole time. It doesn't appear. It was always here, and you were walking too loudly to see it. It stands in the center of the ring, whole and perfect, honey-colored stone rising seventy feet into the sky, its base sunk into the sand as though it had grown there. At its top, in the open belfry, hangs the great bell of Ouna, green-bronze, absolutely still. Above you, the herons stop circling. One by one they glide down and settle on the tower's ledges, folding their wings, as if this were where they had always meant to land.

Failure

You can't do it. Someone shifts their weight, a reed snaps under a boot, a breath catches. And the bell answers: one note, enormous, a wall of bronze sound that slaps the air out of your lungs and flattens the reeds in a ring around you. When your ears stop ringing, the tower is standing in front of you, sand still pattering down around its base as though it had been dropped from the sky a second ago. The herons are gone, scattered to the far bank, complaining.

Cost: each PC is deafened for 1 minute. Lirien's first words to them will be a gentle tease: "You walk very loudly."

The climb

The little door at the tower's base stands open. Inside, the air is cool and absolutely still. The stair spirals up around a hollow core, and slanting shafts of light fall through the narrow windows, and in every shaft the dust is hanging motionless, each mote fixed in place like a star. When someone's boot knocks a pebble off the step, it doesn't fall. It drifts, slowly, turning like a leaf, and settles on the step below as gently as snow. Your heartbeats feel slower in here. Your breathing too. The hymn boards are still on the walls, last week's song numbers chalked on them in a careful hand. You climb seventy feet of stairs, and nobody is out of breath at the top.

The belfry is open to the sky on all four sides. West, across the river and the rooftops, you can see the temple hill and the clean stump where this tower belongs. East, upriver, Silkcliff hangs its silk in the wind. And in the middle of the floor hangs the bell: green-bronze, taller than any of you, its lip a hand's breadth above the boards. On its crown, black against the sky, sits a crow. It looks at you with one bright eye, the way it has looked at you all day.

When the crow speaks Sfillian

Sfillian, against your collar, your jacket stirs. The ThreadWeaver's voice, the dry whisper you haven't heard since the first time: When the crow speaks, listen well.

The crow opens its beak. "Morning, Deitrich! Didn't think we'd see you upright!" It's the voice of the man in the street this morning, perfect down to the laugh. Then, in Marta Fenn's voice: "That bird's been on your knocker since dawn, dear." Then in Korin's deep, careful rumble: "What is on everyone's task list?" It tilts its head, considering you. And then, in a voice of its own, low and clear and round as the bell beneath it: "Forgive me. I have only been listening. I have not yet learned how to begin."

Soundtrack prompt · Cue · Lirien arrives

An orchestral ambient soundtrack of a divine being unfolding out of the note of a great bronze bell, performed by a full live symphony orchestra: one struck tubular bell blooming into luminous divisi strings, a warm French horn and trombone chorale, sweeping concert-harp glissandi and a rising cymbal roll to a soaring but gentle climax, then a curious, playful clarinet and flute theme full of wonder and a little humor. Awe, warmth, ancient kindness. 72 BPM, E major. Real acoustic instruments, concert-hall reverb, no synthesizers, no pads, no electronic sounds. Instrumental, no vocals.

Lirien

The crow steps off the bell into empty air, and doesn't fall. The bell rings, by itself, once: a note so deep and pure you feel it in the roots of your teeth, in the long bones of your legs, in the boards under your feet. And the crow comes apart in it. Not into feathers. The sound takes it, and the black turns to copper, and the copper turns to light, and the light folds and unfolds like someone shaking out a long cloth. What the light shakes out is a person.

Tall. Barefoot. Standing on nothing, then on the boards. Skin the warm, burnished brown of a new copper kettle, and at the edges, the tips of the fingers, the curve of an ear, the line of the jaw, the soft chalky green of an old copper roof, as if they were very old and very new at the same time. A shaved head. Eyes the gray-green of still water. They are wrapped, clumsily, in what you realize is the blue altar cloth from the Temple of Ouna, belted at the waist with a length of frayed bell rope. In one hand, a staff of hammered copper, topped with a tiny figure sitting cross-legged with its eyes closed.

They look down at their own bare feet on the cold boards, wiggle their toes, and their face breaks into an expression of pure astonishment. "Oh," they say. "Cold. That's cold." Then they look up at you and smile, and the smile is the oldest thing you have ever seen.

"Hello. My name is Lirien. I serve Iaru, who you have never heard of, which is not your fault." A pause, while they seem to listen to their own voice with interest. "I fell into your city last night, and I have been watching you all morning, and I would very much like to know you."

Lirien, Herald of Iaru
Emissary of Iaru, the locked-away god of meditation and forgiveness · a patient monk and guide · Devoted, and endlessly curious
Look
Copper skin edged with verdigris; still-water eyes; the temple's altar cloth and a bell-rope belt; a copper staff topped by a meditating figure (Iaru's symbol)
Voice
Unhurried, with long comfortable pauses. Answers questions with questions. Repeats phrases they overheard today. Laughs, delighted, at small mortal things: a sneeze, a puddle, bread.
Wants
To be at the doors when the Reckoning opens them, with good hands on the handles. To walk the river with the party. To learn what hunger is.
Fears
That the seven loud voices will arrive first. That they have forgotten more than they know.
Hiding
Their memory is torn, like Daehir's. They don't know where the other good heralds fell.
Rules
Bound by Vitta's rules: a god's voice may guide but may not fight for mortals. Lirien never attacks. Once per session they may catch someone who is falling.

"I can walk beside you. I cannot walk for you."

Portrait prompt · Lirien (for an actor or token)

Painterly fantasy character portrait, warm late-summer light, muted earth tones with an uncanny emerald-green undertone, soft atmospheric haze, highly detailed, 2:3 aspect ratio. A tall, serene, ageless monk standing barefoot in an open stone belfry beside a great green-bronze bell. Their skin is the warm burnished brown of new copper, shading at the fingertips, ears and jawline into the pale chalky green of verdigris, as though they were both very old and very new. Shaved head, calm gray-green eyes like still water, a faint, ancient, delighted smile. They wear a deep blue altar cloth wrapped awkwardly as a robe, belted with a length of frayed bell rope, and hold a staff of hammered copper topped by a small figure sitting cross-legged in meditation. Dust motes hang motionless in a shaft of gold light around them; a single black crow feather drifts at their feet. Gentle, otherworldly, kind. No text, no watermark.

Four questions

Before they answer anything, Lirien asks each PC one question, as Seraphine did in the one-shot. Each is aimed at something Lirien heard or saw while they were the crow. Wait for each answer; Lirien listens with total attention and never argues.

Ash

Lirien tilts their head toward your sword hand, as if listening to something only they can hear. "Does it still dream about the war?"

Richter

"You hold your fire the way a child holds a bird. Too tight, so it can't get away. Why?" (Seeds Richter's "find his power" thread: the fire answers when he stops gripping it.)

Sfillian

"You're carrying someone. I can see the weight in your shoulders. Who is it?" (Leath, Druder, or himself. Sets up Scene 5.)

Dr. Sharpfoot

"You hesitated at the temple door this morning. How long have the people who pray frightened you?" (Vanril and his cult.)

The lesson of the dust

When someone asks what Lirien is, or what an emissary is. The party knows almost nothing about the gods, so this is their first real lesson in Erta's cosmology.

Lirien sits down cross-legged on the boards, quite suddenly, like a child, and pats the floor beside them. They lift one hand toward a shaft of light where the dust hangs motionless, and breathe out, slowly. The dust begins to move.

Three motes drift out of the haze, brighter than the rest. "In the beginning there were three. One who makes," a mote flares and scatters sparks, "one who breaks," the second swallows a spark and gutters, "and one who weaves." The third mote circles the others, and where it passes, the dust falls into patterns: rings, and rings within rings. "The weaver made a place for the other two to argue without breaking everything. A ring." The dust closes into a slowly turning circle the size of a dinner plate. "This one. You call it Erta. The old word is Certamen. It means the contest."

Around the ring, twenty-one tiny lights kindle, one by one. "The three made gods. Seven each. And the gods did what children do with a toy they all want." The lights dart and collide; the ring shudders; motes fall away into darkness. "So the weaver made rules. Every five thousand years the ring turns, and the gods contest for it. When it's over, the winners stay lit. And the losers…" Ten lights keep burning. The rest dim to embers, and the dust closes around each one like a tiny cage. "…wait. Locked away, until the next turning."

Lirien touches one of the caged embers, very gently. It is copper-colored. "This is mine. Iaru. He teaches stillness, and forgiveness. Your great-grandparents' great-grandparents stopped saying his name. A god cannot walk in the world, even when the ring turns. So each sends a voice instead." They spread their hands, palms up, presenting themselves. "A herald. Your scholars would say an emissary. A god's voice that has learned to walk."

The ring is turning faster now. Here and there, among the lit lights and the caged ones alike, seven are glowing an ugly, smoky red. "The ring is turning again, and the doors are opening a crack. Not every voice coming through is kind. Your children sing about some of them, I think. Zara. Galtor. Rilien, who wears my name with its letters turned around." For a moment Lirien's face goes very old. "I am one of the others." They breathe in. The dust falls all at once, like a curtain dropping, and is only dust again.

Lirien's answers · for the questions players will ask
They askLirien saysDM truth
Are you a god?"No. I'm what a god says when he can't be in the room."Emissary of Iaru (canon).
Why take the tower?"I was falling. I needed something that was already listening. A bell is a prayer that doesn't need words. I fell into its note, and the tower came with me, so I set it down where it would hurt no one. I'll give it back."The green meteor (S49) was Lirien. They spent the night "arriving" in the bell.
Why us?(Looking at Ash.) "Iaru whispered: find the sword that dreams. I followed the dreaming. It led to your door."[OPEN] Proposal: Daehir.
What's the Reckoning?"The turning of the ring. When it turns, the locked doors open a crack, and whoever holds the handles decides who comes through."The 5,000-year contest; Titans; the Umbral Order.
The Umbral Order?"Mortal hands, holding doors for the seven loudest voices. They're building giants for their gods to wear. You've seen the giants' footprints."The golem "tests" at Tunstead and Fanfoss.
Can you stop them? Fight with us?"No. The weaver's rule: a god's voice may guide; it may not carry. If I lift a sword for you, I break the rule, and the rule breaks me. I can walk beside you."Lirien is a guide, not a combatant.
The Whisperwind Halls?"A library that remembers the last turning. Its keepers will ask you for a pledge. If we walk far enough together, I may remember the words."new Proposal: Lirien can teach the pledge.
Can you bring Lewis back?(A long silence.) "No. But tell me about him, and I'll remember him for as long as I exist. That's longer than stone."Seeds the Caldwell beat in Scene 4.
Why are you green?"Copper turns green when it has been waiting a very long time. I am very old and very new. It shows at the edges."The verdigris on the tower's cut.
What do you want?"To walk up the river with you. To learn what bread is. To be there when the doors open."Lirien joins the expedition.

Shadowsteel Ashvoice changer on

Lirien looks at Ash for a long moment, and you have the strangest feeling that they are not looking at you at all, but through you, at something sitting behind your eyes. "Hello, Shadowsteel," they say gently. "You've slept a long time."

Inside your mind, Daehir goes utterly still, like an animal that has realized it's been seen. When he speaks, it's barely a whisper. "You. The staff. You were on the hill at Bantambar."

"I was." Lirien's voice is very soft. "You don't remember what you did there."

A silence that goes on a long time. "…No."

"Good," says Lirien. "Then there's room to become something else. Iaru has already forgiven you. I'm still deciding." Then they smile at Ash, warm and sudden as sunlight. "Don't worry. I like him better asleep than awake. But I like you very much."

Daehir's title is "the Bane of Bantambar" (canon). That Lirien was there is new, and a strong hook for Ash's arc.

Quiet moment · the belfry

"Sit," Lirien says. "Not for long. Only long enough to hear what you're carrying."

You sit on the edge of the belfry with your legs over the drop, the way children sit on a harbor wall. Below you, the herons stand on the tower's ledges, utterly still. The river slides by, brown and gold, and the wind brings you the smell of reeds and warm sand. Upstream, Silkcliff's threads stir and shine, and from its tallest crane hangs something wrapped in white, turning very slowly. Lirien closes their eyes. The bell above you hums one note, so low and soft it's like a cat purring in another room. Nobody speaks for a while. It is the first time any of you have sat still since Harmonia.

Lirien asks one or two · no rolls

  • "Who is the hardest person for you to forgive?" (For Sfillian, the true answer may be himself.)
  • "If you could leave one thing on this tower and walk away from it, what would it be?"
  • Richter "What did your father's hands look like?"
  • Sharpfoot "Did you forgive your partner, or only stop him?"

Giving it back

Lirien stands, and lays one copper palm flat against the bell. "I borrowed this. Time to give it back. You'll want to be standing on sand."

You climb down. Lirien doesn't; you see them step off the top of the stair and drift past you down the hollow core, as unhurried as a falling leaf, and they're waiting on the sand when you come out. The herons lift off the ledges all together, a gray cloud of wings. Lirien touches the tower with the tip of the copper staff. The stone goes clear, like honey held up to a lamp, and then it isn't stone at all but light, green-gold and soft, and the whole tower rises out of the sand like a held breath let go. It drifts west over the river, over the warehouses, over the rooftops of the seven hills, slow as a lantern on a pond, and settles onto the temple hill. For a moment, nothing.

Then the great bell of Ouna rings out over Inkwich. And then the bells of Alos answer it, and Urra's, and Eone's, and Rulir's, until every bell on the tallest hill is ringing at once, and from the docks and the streets and the open windows of the city you can hear people shouting and laughing and crying. The herons settle back onto their island one by one.

Lirien sneezes. They look utterly astonished. "What was that?"

Lirien's gift

Before you leave the island, Lirien unwinds the bell-rope belt from their waist, and four copper beads that were certainly not there a moment ago slide down it into their palm. "For when you can't hear yourselves think. Hold one and be still, and you'll know where I am." They press one into each of your hands. The bead is warm, as if someone has been holding it for a very long time.

Copper Bead of Iaru
Consumable · trinket · uncommon · ×4

Once, when you fail a Wisdom, Intelligence or Charisma save, crush it to reroll. Hold it still for a minute to sense whether Lirien is within a mile, and which way.

Quick reference · Stillwater Eyot
Look closerHeron prints all leading away; the perfect ring of flattened reeds. From the belfry: the temple hill and its stump to the west; upstream to the east, Silkcliff, with a white cocoon on its tallest crane (→ Scene 5).
HiddenDC 14 Perception from the belfry: the white shape on Silkcliff's crane moves, as if something inside it shifted.
SensesGlassy water, herons on one leg · a note felt in the teeth · reeds, warm sand, lilac · dust that won't fall · copper on the tongue
Who's hereMags Pellow new: ferrywoman; eats onions like apples; won't set foot on the eyot until the herons do.The herons: they settle only once the party is still.
On returnAfter Lirien returns the tower: the herons are back. By next spring the flattened ring will bloom lilac, and children will call it the Herald's Seat.

Ask the table

  • What do your characters actually believe about the gods, now that one has sneezed at them?
  • Ash: does Daehir say anything to you after the herald has gone quiet?
  • Who gives Lirien their cloak?

If the party…

Attacks LirienLirien doesn't defend; the blow passes through copper light. "That's fair. I'd be frightened of me too." They stay.
Brought Korin or LiraKorin speaks Celestial and kneels. Lirien: "Please don't. My knees don't work properly yet either."
Asks Lirien to keep the tower"It isn't mine to keep. Most things aren't."
Clues: the emissaries are gods' voices; seven of them are hostile; Lirien and Daehir share a pastClock: the Emissary clock is retired (Lirien has joined the party)
Leads to · Scene 4 · 52 paths
Bringing a herald homeGo to Scene 4 →

NudgeLirien is barefoot, shivering in an altar cloth, and hungry for the first time in five thousand years. Their stomach growls; they look down at it in wonder. "There's an ache here. Is this grief?" "That's hunger." "Oh! How wonderful. What do we do about it?" Boots, a coat, bread: the Caldwells. This is the "return to the shop."

Mags poles you back to the bank, and you walk Lirien home through Inkwich. It takes far longer than it should. They stop for everything: a puddle (they step in it on purpose, gasp, and step in it again), a dog (they bow to it, and it bows back, as far as dogs can), the smell of bread from an open window (they stand under it with their eyes closed until someone takes their elbow). People stare at the barefoot stranger wrapped in a blue altar cloth, and Lirien beams at every one of them. And all the way, from every quarter of the city, the bells are still ringing. Then you turn the last corner.

Then read the Scene 4 arrival (or "Back again," if they've already been).

Straight upstreamGo to Scene 5 →

NudgeOnly if the light is already going. From the belfry they've seen the cocoon on Silkcliff's crane. Lirien won't come: "He invited you, not me." They'll wait among the herons and turn up at the Senro Hotel later. Mags will pole the party to the north bank for another 2 copper.

Mags poles you to the north bank in silence, chewing her onion, and drops you on a strip of shingle below the last boatyards. Behind you, out on the eyot, a small copper-and-green figure stands among the herons, waving, until the reeds hide them. You follow the bank path upstream past overturned hulls and cold tar pots, the shipwrights gone home for the night. The wind off the water picks up, cool and smelling of reeds. Ahead, the path bends around the last boatyard.

Then read the Scene 5 arrival.

The Shop & the Old Sailor

Late afternoonCaldwell store & Senro Hotel
Who: Jacob & Alice Caldwell, the baby, Admiral Biscuit, Senro Sero, LirienLeans on: Ash Richter Sfillian
Why they're here

Art prompt · The Caldwell store

Painterly fantasy concept art, warm late-summer light over a river-trade city, muted earth tones with bright silk accents and an uncanny emerald-green undertone, soft atmospheric haze, cinematic composition, highly detailed environment, 16:9 aspect ratio. The warm interior of a well-loved two-story merchant's shop seen from just inside the door. Shelves of goods climb the timber walls: coils of rope, brass lanterns, folded oilcloth, sacks of peppercorns and dried lavender, a row of sturdy boots. Along the counter, neat rows of small potion bottles in ruby, amber and pale green glow softly, each with a second little label tied to its neck. A worn ledger lies open with a pencil beside it. Tucked behind the counter, a simple wooden cradle with a knitted blanket. In the wide front window, a fat orange cat sleeps in a sunbeam among the lanterns. Through the glass, the street outside and, next door, an old sailor's hotel with a polished brass ship's lantern hanging over its door. A small cracked brass bell above the shop door. Warm, golden afternoon light, dust drifting in the sunbeams; homely, gentle and quietly sad. No people, no text, no watermark.

Painterly fantasy concept art, warm late-summer light over a river-trade city, muted earth tones with bright silk accents and an uncanny emerald-green undertone, soft atmospheric haze, cinematic composition, highly detailed environment, 16:9 aspect ratio. No people, no text, no watermark.

Soundtrack prompt · The Shop & the Old Sailor

An orchestral ambient soundtrack of a cozy merchant's shop and an old sailor's inn on a golden late afternoon, performed by a live chamber orchestra: a tender solo cello, warm clarinet and bassoon, plucked strings and concert harp, a lullaby melody on celesta, and a gentle sea-shanty tune passed between solo violin and low strings, with moments of quiet grief. Homely, bittersweet, with small sparks of wonder. 76 BPM, G major with minor turns. Real acoustic instruments, concert-hall reverb, no synthesizers, no pads, no electronic sounds. Loopable, instrumental, no vocals.

Some places you come back to and find smaller than you remembered. The Caldwell store isn't one of them. Two stories of warm timber and wide windows, with a fat orange cat asleep in a sunbeam among the lanterns, exactly where a fat orange cat was asleep the first day you walked into Inkwich with mud on your boots. Next door, the brass ship's lantern still hangs over the Senro Hotel, polished to a shine by an old sailor who never stopped keeping watch.

The bell over the shop door has the same small crack in it, so it doesn't ring so much as clank, cheerfully, like it's glad to see you. Inside, the smell carries you backward: oiled leather and lamp oil, dried lavender and peppercorns, the sharp tang of Thomas Caldwell's potions in neat rows by the counter, each bottle with a second, smaller label stuck to the back.

Something is new: a wooden cradle behind the counter, and the small sounds of someone very new to the world grumbling in their sleep. Standing over the ledger, pencil behind his ear, is Jacob Caldwell. He looks up when the bell clanks and grins, wide and quick and easy, and for one terrible second it is exactly Lewis's grin. "Well, look what the river dragged in! Where's that brother of mine? He owes me eleven silver and a…"

He stops. His eyes go from face to face. Three he knows. One, an elderly tortle in a white hat, he doesn't. And the one he's looking for isn't there.

Behind you, the bell clanks a second time as Lirien ducks in under the lintel, sees the orange cat in the window, and stops dead, the way you'd stop in a cathedral. "What," they whisper, "is that?" The cat opens one eye, considers the herald of a forgotten god, and closes it again.

The cracked bell clanks again, cheerfully, as if it had been expecting you. Jacob looks up from the counter with a smile, sees who you've brought this time, a barefoot stranger in a temple altar cloth gazing at the lanterns as if they were stars, and very slowly puts down his pencil.

Jacob hears

No checks. Let the players decide what to say. Don't rescue them from the silences.

Jacob doesn't say anything for a long while. He sets the pencil down on the ledger, very precisely, lining it up with the edge of the page. Behind him the baby fusses, and without looking he reaches back and sets the cradle rocking with two fingers, the way you do something you've done a thousand times in the dark. Alice has come to the doorway of the back room with one hand over her mouth.

"He owed me eleven silver," Jacob says at last, to the ledger. "And a story. He was always going to tell me how he got that scar on his chin, and he never did, because he said it was better as a mystery." He laughs, once, a terrible little sound. Then he looks up, eyes wet, voice very steady. "I suppose one of you will have to tell me the story now. How it happened. All of it. I'd rather know."

Jacob nods slowly, and then tells you one. "When he was nine, Lewis climbed the Silkcliff catwalks on a dare. All the way to the top, at night, in his stockings so the tenders wouldn't hear him on the boards. Did you know the top huts all have little hatches in the back walls, for reaching the cranes? He found that out. Came down with a cage of silkworms under his shirt and let them loose in our mother's sewing room." He wipes his face with the heel of his hand. "She chased him round the block with a broom. He was laughing the whole time."

The back hatches give the party a hidden way into Druder's hut. Whoever uses them gets advantage on their Six Seconds action in Scene 5. If they hedge or lie to Jacob ("he's on a job"), he believes them because he wants to. Log it; it will hurt later.

Dressing a herald needs Lirien

It's Alice who takes charge, in the end, because somebody has to. Within minutes Lirien is sitting on a flour sack with a wool shirt over the altar cloth and three pairs of boots lined up in front of them like suitors. They hate the first pair. They are deeply suspicious of the second. They put on the third, stand up, take four careful steps across the floorboards, and turn around with tears standing in their eyes. "They hold my feet," they say. "Like hands."

Jacob offers them a peppermint from the jar on the counter, the way he offers one to everyone. Lirien puts it in their mouth, goes very still, and has to sit back down on the flour sack. The orange cat, which has not moved for anyone in eleven years, climbs down out of the window, crosses the shop, and settles in Lirien's lap like a loaf of bread, purring loud enough to rattle the potion bottles. Behind the counter the baby has started to cry, thin and furious. Lirien lifts their head and hums, one low note, the same note you felt on the eyot. The crying stops. The baby gives a small, astonished hiccup, and falls asleep.

Lirien looks at Jacob for a long moment. "Someone is missing from this room. I can feel the shape where they used to stand." And, if Jacob knows: "Tell me his story. I'll remember it for as long as I exist. That's longer than stone."

Thomas's potions at cost, or Jacob won't take coin

Each bottle has its side effects written on a second label on the back, in Thomas's tiny, apologetic handwriting. new

Caldwell's Mending Draught
Consumable · potion · common · 50 gp

Regain 2d4 + 2 HP. Side effect: DC 10 Con save or speak only Halfling for 10 minutes.

Riverman's Tonic
Consumable · potion · common · 30 gp

8 hours: advantage on Con saves against exhaustion; rowing tires you no faster than walking. Side effect: your voice booms like a foghorn for an hour.

Lamp-Eye Drops
Consumable · potion · common · 40 gp

Darkvision 60 ft for 1 hour (+30 ft if you have it). Side effect: your eyes glow faintly green.

Thomas's Burn Salve
Consumable · potion · common · 15 gp

Regain 1d4 HP and soothe a burn. Side effect: smells powerfully of mint for a day. The jar for Oakhallow's hand.

The old sailor

Senro's common room is low and dim and smells of pipe smoke and old rope, and every inch of its walls is covered with the sea: charts gone brown with age, a harpoon over the fireplace, a ship in a bottle the size of a loaf of bread, a carved mermaid figurehead with a chipped nose leaning in the corner like a guest who came early to a party. The old sailor himself is at his corner table with the broadsheet, exactly where you left him months ago, as if he's been anchored there. He looks up, sees you, and starts to smile.

And then, Sfillian, in your pack, something begins to glow. The Storm Seer's Lamp, the one Senro gave you, is lit from inside without anyone touching it. Its glass has gone the soft, flat green of still water, and the little silver needle inside has swung all the way over to a mark you've never once seen it touch: dead calm.

Senro sets down the broadsheet very carefully. "Fifty years at sea," he says, "and I never saw that lamp show dead calm." His eyes move past you to the stranger in the doorway. Lirien is looking at the walls, the charts and the harpoon and the little ship in its bottle, with an expression of complete and helpless wonder. "What," Lirien says softly, "is all this water?"

Senro looks at them for a long moment. Then he pulls out the chair beside him. "Sit down, friend. That," he says, "is the sea."

Senro Sero
Retired sailor; keeps the Senro Hotel next to the Caldwell store · Friendly
Voice
Slow, salty, few words; every sentence sounds like a weather report
History
Gave the party the Storm Seer's Lamp and the paired message tubes (S15)
Wants
To see one more wonder before the tide takes him. He's just met one.
Beats
1. Tells Lirien about the sea (no roll; let it breathe). 2. "That plum-coat gent who was asking about the bard? Saw him at the Hungry Owl, buying something off Kailu, wrapped in silk. It moved." (Druder's moth cocoons; Kailu is the black-market elf the party freed in S8.) 3. "Your leonin wants a boat. I've sent word to Brannock, old shipmate. Dawn tomorrow, east wharf." 4. If they haven't found the tower: "Stillwater Eyot. The herons left it at midnight, every one. Fifty years I've watched that river; herons don't leave." 5. To Lirien: "First night's free for anyone who's never seen the sea."

"Fifty years at sea, and I never saw that."

Korin meets the herald optional

Korin finds you at Senro's as the afternoon turns gold, the smell of the docks still on his coat. He stops in the doorway. His mane lifts, all of it, like a cat's fur in a storm, and his golden eyes go wide. Slowly, as if his body has decided before he has, the leader of the Augury goes down on one knee on Senro's floorboards and says something low and reverent in a language none of you speak. Lirien answers him in the same tongue, then switches, gently, to yours. "Please don't. My knees don't work properly yet either."

Lirien stays

When you rise to leave, Lirien doesn't. "The man on the cliff invited you," they say, "not me. And I know what happens when a god's voice walks into a mortal quarrel: everyone loses something they didn't bet." They wrap both hands around the mug of something hot Senro has put in front of them and breathe in the steam with their eyes closed. "I'll be here. Senro is going to tell me about whales."

Quick reference · Caldwell store & Senro Hotel
Look closerThomas's potions, side effects on the back. A letter from James pinned up, bragging about his Bursar seat. The cradle. At Senro's: the Storm Seer's Lamp, gone green.
SensesSunbeams and a sleeping cat · the cracked bell, a fussing baby · leather, lavender, peppercorns, pipe smoke · the peppermint Jacob always offers
Who's hereJacob Caldwell: Lewis's brother; warm, joking, the most honest man in Inkwich.Alice and the baby [OPEN] name.Admiral Biscuit: the shop cat. Fat, orange, immovable, except for Lirien.Senro Sero: see his card above.
On returnAfter they tell Jacob: a black ribbon on the door and Lewis's portrait in the window. After tonight: Lirien has a room at the Senro Hotel whenever they're in Inkwich.

Ask the table

  • What's a story about Lewis only your character knows?
  • Who keeps Jacob's letter to James and Nancy, and where?
  • Dr. Sharpfoot: you never met Lewis. What do you make of these people mourning him?

If the party…

Comes before finding the towerRun "Jacob hears" and Senro's beats 2 to 4, then send them east. They'll be back with Lirien.
Wants Lirien at SilkcliffLirien comes only as far as the foot of the cliff path, and won't intervene in Scene 5.
Lies to JacobHe's cheerful and generous. Jacob's letter becomes "for Lewis." It will hurt later.
Clues: Druder bought silk-wrapped things from Kailu; the back hatches at Silkcliff; Brannock's boat at dawn
Leads to · Scene 2 · 3 · 53 paths
Up to the temple hillGo to Scene 2 →

NudgeAlice presses a small jar into someone's hand: "Thomas's burn salve. They're saying Mother Oakhallow burned her hand on that glass. She was good to us when Jacob's father was ill. Would you take it up to her?" (The gift makes Oakhallow Friendly.)

You carry the little jar up the hill like an offering. The streets climb toward the temples in tiers, and with every tier the city gets older: timber gives way to stone, stone to older stone, and the shop signs change from painted boards to carved ones whose words have long since weathered away. A pair of pilgrims up from the countryside ask you the way, and you realize you're all going to the same place. At the foot of the tallest hill, the streets give up, and the stairs begin.

Then read the Scene 2 arrival.

East, to the riverGo to Scene 3 →

NudgeSenro, pointing east with the stem of his pipe: "Stillwater Eyot. The herons left it at midnight, every one. Fifty years I've watched that river from my window. Herons don't leave."

Senro points you east with the stem of his pipe, and you go: downhill through the warehouse streets where the buried river breathes up through the grates, past chandlers and rope-walks and a cooper's yard stacked with new barrels like a wall of drums, out past the last warehouse, where the cobbles give way to a dirt track and the city's noise drops behind you. A stray gull follows you for a while, then thinks better of it. Ahead, the path drops through a stand of willows toward the water.

Then read the Scene 3 arrival.

To SilkcliffGo to Scene 5 →

NudgeThe light is going, and the note said dusk. Jacob's story of the back hatches is fresh, and so is Senro's warning about whatever was moving in that silk.

As you leave, old Senro is out on his step with a taper, lighting the brass ship's lantern over his door the way he does every evening, whether there's a ship coming or not. Through the window behind him, Lirien sits at the corner table with both hands wrapped around a mug, watching you go. They raise it to you. You walk east, out through the warehouse district where the river breathes up through the grates, past the last tanneries and rope-walks, out onto the river road. The wind off the water picks up, cool and smelling of reeds. Ahead, the road bends around the last boatyard.

Then read the Scene 5 arrival.
