sections.html:
5

Druder's Last Act

DuskSilkcliff, the top hut
Who: Druder Craggy, Leath, Knuckle Garro, Spool Dace, Mirela, Old Bett Loom, FerrisLeans on: Sfillian, with a job for everyone in the last six seconds
Why they're here

The note: "Silkcliff, at dusk." Everything else they learned today points here too: the cocoon on the crane seen from the eyot (Scene 3), Senro's silk-wrapped purchase from Kailu, and Jacob's back hatches (Scene 4).

How it must end · DM only

Druder escapes with Leath, by magic, and the session ends on that. The players decide what it costs him and what they snatch from it, never whether he goes.

  • The magic: a Greater Moth-Step Cocoon, bought from Kailu with Opalcrest money. Crushed, it releases a storm of white silk moths around Druder and one creature he's holding. Six seconds later both come apart into moths and re-form up to 300 feet away: in the skiff waiting in the reeds below. Like misty step, but for two, and further.
  • The timing: he crushes it at his curtain line. Everyone gets one action (Six Seconds), then they're gone. Once crushed, it needs no will: holding or downing Druder doesn't stop it.
  • The hostage: Druder grips Leath's wrist through the cage bars. Anyone who reaches them finds a knife at Leath's throat.
  • What they can win: words with Leath · Leath's scarf · a wound Druder will carry · a captured thug who names the destination · the skiff's heading and crest · the lesser cocoon that falls from Druder's coat · and Sfillian's truth, spoken aloud.
  • Backstop: Druder carries a second greater cocoon up his sleeve. If the table finds a way the first one can't cover, he uses the second.
  • Lirien stays at Senro's (Scene 4). If they insisted on coming, they stop at the foot of the path: "This is not my door."
Art prompt · Silkcliff at dusk

Painterly fantasy concept art, warm late-summer light over a river-trade city, muted earth tones with bright silk accents and an uncanny emerald-green undertone, soft atmospheric haze, cinematic composition, highly detailed environment, 16:9 aspect ratio. A sheer hundred-foot cliff of pale gray shale rising straight out of a wide river at dusk, seen from the riverbank below. Hundreds of fine silk threads hang down the cliff face from cages suspended on crane arms, each thread catching the last of the sunset and glowing copper, rose and molten gold, so the whole cliff shimmers like the strings of an enormous harp. A zigzag web of narrow wooden catwalks and ladders clings to the rock. Along the top edge, a row of small single-story tending huts with lanterns just being lit, their wooden crane arms silhouetted against a bronze and violet sky like the necks of herons. The largest hut has its great loading doors thrown open; from its crane, out over the drop, hangs a wardrobe-sized iron cage wrapped tightly in white raw silk. At the cliff's foot, half hidden in the reeds, a small dark skiff waits. A few pale moths drift in the dusk air. Wind-blown silk, long shadows, the air of a stage set for a final act. No people, no text, no watermark.

Soundtrack prompt · Silkcliff at dusk

An orchestral ambient soundtrack of a silk-strung cliff at dusk turned into a stage for a cruel performance, performed by a live orchestra with a featured solo lute: a melancholy, slightly out-of-tune lute melody over pizzicato strings and sustained low cellos, fragments of a theatrical waltz in the woodwinds, tension rising through tremolo violins, muted brass and soft timpani rolls. Bittersweet and menacing, like a final act about to begin. 3/4 time, 90 BPM, A minor. Real acoustic instruments, concert-hall reverb, no synthesizers, no pads, no electronic sounds. Loopable, instrumental, no vocals.

You've seen Silkcliff before, from the road, in daylight. You've never seen it like this. The sun is going down behind you over Inkwich, and its last light strikes the cliff full on, and every one of the hundreds of silk threads hanging down the gray shale has caught fire. Not literally, but they glow, copper and rose and molten gold, swaying in the river wind so the whole cliff seems to shimmer and breathe, like the strings of an enormous harp someone has only just stopped playing.

The tenders are finishing for the day: small dark figures on the catwalks moving with the casual, terrifying grace of people who have walked a hundred feet above the ground every day of their lives, calling to each other in a sing-song cant. One is laughing. Lanterns are lit along the top of the cliff, one after another, and the crane arms reaching over the drop are silhouetted against the sky like the necks of herons.

The wind here never stops. It pours up the cliff from the river and thrums through the silk, and if you stand still, it makes a sound: a low, wavering chord, felt more in your chest than heard. The tenders say Silkcliff sings at dusk. Tonight it's singing something sad.

At the very top, the largest hut has every lantern lit and its door wide open, and drifting out over the drop comes the sound of a lute. Someone is playing a song you know. It's one of the first songs you ever learned, Sfillian. You learned it from the man who is playing it.

The stage

Inside, someone has turned the long, low hut into a theater. Every lantern hangs from the rafters, and bolts of undyed silk drape from the beams like curtains, so the room glows soft and gold and swims with shadows as the silk stirs. Chairs are set out in a neat row. Four of them. Exactly four.

The far wall isn't there: two great loading doors thrown wide onto the dusk, and beyond them nothing at all, just a hundred feet of air and the river turning bronze below. A crane arm juts out into that emptiness, and from its hook hangs something the size of a wardrobe, wrapped tight in raw silk, turning slowly in the wind.

And in front of the open doors, on a stool, his face in shadow, a man is playing a lute. Badly; he has to. He's propped the neck against the stump of his right wrist, fretting with his left hand and plucking with a quill clenched in his teeth, and the song comes out slow and broken and strange. But you know it, Sfillian. You learned it on the floor of a tavern in Dunnling Grove with your back against this man's knee.

He finishes the verse. He takes the quill from his teeth and looks up, and the lantern light catches his face: older, thinner, ruined around the eyes by drink, and lit from inside with the purest, most uncomplicated joy you have ever seen. "Sfillian," says Druder Craggy. "My boy. You came."

Druder Craggy
Disgraced bard; Sfillian's old mentor; the Opalcrests' tool · Hostile, and delighted
Look
Threadbare plum coat; right sleeve pinned; a pale moth crawling out of his cuff now and then
Wants
One line: Sfillian's confession, in front of witnesses
Hiding
He's started to like Leath. And the cocoon in his coat is pulsing.
Stats
Spy, AC 13, Wis save +2. He's here to perform, not fight.

"I taught you every chord you know, boy. Let's see if you remember the last one."

He sets the lute down with enormous care, as if it were a sleeping child, rises, and spreads his arms wide, left hand open, right sleeve empty below the elbow. "Look at you! Look at that jacket! Somebody's been doing well for himself." He's laughing, actually laughing, and his eyes are wet. "Two years I've pictured this exact moment, and you've exceeded every one of them. You brought friends! An audience!" He sweeps his arm at the chairs. "Please. Sit. It's rude to stand through a performance."

He introduces his stagehands with a flourish: a big, slow man by the door, a wiry one by the crane. "Don't mind them. They're only here to make sure nobody leaves before the final bow." As he talks, a small white moth crawls out of his cuff, flutters up toward the lanterns, and is joined by another. He waves them away fondly. "And don't mind the moths. Silk country. They get into everything."

The reveal

Druder takes hold of a silk cord hanging from the rafters and gives it one theatrical tug. Out over the drop, the wrapping on the hanging shape comes loose all at once and peels away into the wind like the petals of a flower opening, streaming out over the river, glowing in the last light.

Inside is a tending cage: iron bars and a plank floor. And sitting cross-legged on the planks, knees pulled to his chest and a long blue scarf wound around his neck, is Leath. He's thinner. His hair has grown out. There's a fading bruise on one cheekbone. But he's alive, and he's looking at you, and his face does something complicated: hope, and fear, and then, because he is your brother, a crooked, terrified, defiant little smile.

"Hey, Sfil," he calls across the gap. His voice cracks. "Took you long enough."

Behind you, Druder sighs happily. "Isn't it wonderful? I do love a family reunion. Now, Sfillian. I don't want money, and I don't want your brother. I want a line. One line, spoken aloud, in front of witnesses." His voice goes soft. "Did you do it? Did you put me in that bed with the Lady Opalcrest?"

The confessionSfillian · roleplay, no rollOthers: DC 13 Insight to read Druder

The wind thrums through the silk. Out over the drop, Leath is waiting too. Sfillian, what do you tell him? (Let the silence stretch. Lirien's question from the belfry may still be in the room.)

Confesses

Druder doesn't move. Then he closes his eyes and lets out a breath that seems to go on forever, and something in his shoulders gives way, as if he's been holding up a great weight for two years and has only just been allowed to set it down. When he opens his eyes, the joy is gone. What's left is quieter, and much worse. "Thank you. You'd be amazed how much that was worth." He looks at Leath, then back at you. "It doesn't change the ending, my boy. The Opalcrests own this story now. But I'll look after him. On my honor, such as it is."

From here on, Druder treats Leath gently.

Lies or refuses

Druder's smile doesn't falter. It widens, stretching until it's a terrible thing to look at. "Ah. Well. I'd hoped you'd grown up." He turns toward the open doors and the cage swinging over the drop. "Then we'll have to keep rehearsing. Come and find me, boy. Upriver. I'll leave the lights on."

Druder becomes a true enemy on the river.

Soundtrack prompt · Cue · The curtain

An orchestral ambient soundtrack of a magical escape inside a blizzard of white moths, performed by a full live symphony orchestra: high violins and flutes in rapid, fluttering trills and runs, glittering harp and celesta, a racing pulse of cellos, basses and timpani building to a sudden cut-off, then a lone, fading lute phrase answered by one soft, low cello note. Frantic, beautiful, heartbreaking. 120 BPM falling to silence, D minor. Real acoustic instruments, concert-hall reverb, no synthesizers, no pads, no electronic sounds. Instrumental, no vocals.

The curtain

Druder Craggy takes one running step and leaps out through the loading doors, into nothing, and lands lightly on the roof of the swinging cage like a man who has practiced it a hundred times. He reaches down through the bars and closes his hand around Leath's wrist. With the other hand he holds something up for you to see: a cocoon the size of a hen's egg, white and soft and faintly, horribly, pulsing.

"Ladies and gentlemen," he calls, "thank you. You've been a marvelous audience."

He crushes it. The moths come out of his fist like smoke from a fire, white and endless: hundreds, then thousands, pouring out between his fingers faster than anything that size could hold, swirling up around him and down through the bars, a blizzard of soft white wings boiling in the dusk. You can still see them in the middle of it: Druder's grin, Leath's wide eyes. But their edges are fraying. Druder's coat is coming apart into wings. Leath's hand, reaching toward you through the bars, is coming apart into wings.

Six secondsOne round · every PC acts onceThen they're gone, whatever happens

Everything below is something the party can win. The moths take Druder and Leath at the end of the round.

A PC tries…CheckWhat it wins
Shoot or blast Drudervs AC 13A wound he'll carry: a scar across the face, a bolt in the shoulder. The moths take him anyway.
Hold Person, or knock him downWis save +2He's held, and furious; the cocoon is already crushed and needs no will. He goes anyway.
Dispel Magic on the swarmDC 15 spellcasting check (auto at 5th level)The moths scatter for a heartbeat. Leath half re-forms, clasps the nearest hand, and presses the scarf and a whisper into it (below). Then the swarm takes him back.
Leap for the cage (Misty Step, Jump, a desperate grab)DC 15 Athl./Acro. · auto with teleportThey reach the bars. Druder: "Let go, or the moths take you too." If they hold on, the swarm carries them along and drops them 20 feet over the river: a cold swim, no damage. Leath whispers to them on the way.
Grab the wiry thugDC 13 AthleticsSpool Dace (Bandit) captured. He talks within minutes (below).
Watch the reeds belowDC 14 PerceptionA skiff with an opal-in-a-crescent crest on its stern, and its heading: east, upriver.
Catch what fallsDC 12 Dex (Acrobatics)As the swarm thickens, a smaller cocoon tumbles from Druder's coat and bounces toward the edge. Missed, it lodges on a catwalk below, where they can retrieve it later.
Sfillian shouts to LeathNoneLeath answers (in the cliffhanger).

Stats if needed: Knuckle Garro (Thug, flees once Druder's gone) · Spool Dace (Bandit, surrenders when grappled) · Mirela (Scout, in the skiff below).

"He's taking me upriver. There's a buyer. I'll leave you signs. Look for my knots, Sfil. Three knots, like Da taught us."

Spool Dace talks

"The Opalcrests are paying. There's a buyer upriver. A trading post called Wrenmouth new, below the upper falls. That's all I know, I swear on my mother." (True.)

Moth-Step Cocoon
Consumable · trinket · uncommon · the one that falls

Bonus action: crush it, dissolve into silk moths, and reappear up to 30 ft away (as misty step). One use.

Leath's Scarf
Loot · gear · left on the cage, or pressed into a hand

Faded blue wool, one end knotted three times, deliberately. His first sign.

Cliffhanger

And then the storm folds in on itself, like a hand closing, and they're gone. The cage swings on its hook over the drop, empty, creaking. Snagged on one of its bars, a long blue scarf flutters in the wind.

The moths pour over the edge of the cliff like a waterfall of snow, a white river of wings tumbling a hundred feet down the darkening rock to the reeds at its foot. And there, in a small dark skiff, they come back together: a man in a plum coat, sprawled laughing in the stern, and a boy on his knees in the bottom of the boat. The masked figure at the pole is already pushing hard, and the skiff slides out of the last light and into the black mouth of a side channel.

A voice comes up to you from the dark water, cracked and desperate and stubborn as only a brother's can be. "SFIL! Upriver! He's taking me upriver! I'll leave you…"

Then Druder's laughter, warm and delighted, rolling across the water. Then the reeds close behind the skiff, and there is nothing at all but the wind, singing in the silk.

On the back of Sfillian's hand, a single white moth settles. It slowly opens its wings, and closes them again.

Quick reference · Silkcliff
Layout100-ft shale cliff. Tending huts along the top, each with a crane and a cage over the drop. Catwalks zigzag down the face. Each top hut has a small back hatch for reaching the crane (Jacob's story). Reeds and a side channel at the cliff's foot, where the skiff waits.
HiddenDC 14 Insight the "tenders" by the big hut have clean hands (thugs) · DC 16 Investigation or Insight something in Druder's coat is pulsing; moths keep crawling from his cuff (a teleport trinket) · DC 18 Sleight of Hand to lift it before the reveal: his smile slips, then he draws the backstop from his sleeve, and the stolen one is the party's
SensesGlowing threads, heron-necked cranes · the cliff's low chord, a lute, the tenders' cant · river water, wet shale, lantern oil · catwalks that sway; wind that never stops
Who's hereOld Bett Loom: silk tender, sharp-eyed gossip, two fingers missing. In daylight: "The fancy gent renting the top hut keeps his right arm in his cloak. Something in the big cage sings at night."Ferris: her grandson, fourteen, fearless on the catwalks; knows the back hatches.
On returnThe top hut stands empty, the cage still swinging. Bett has kept anything they left behind.

If the party…

Scouts in daylightHut locked, cage wrapped. They can post someone in the reeds by the skiff: one extra action at the bottom (strike Mirela; hear Leath's full whisper as he re-forms).

A flat-bottomed punt is drawn up at the island's edge. Far behind, on the near bank, willows and the last warehouses of a city on seven hills; upstream, a pale cliff strung with silk threads.
